opus-5.5.text:
I think once the base models have basically caught up with each other, the real differentiation moves to post-training, and especially to how you train agents. For a while, a lot of people believed that if you just scaled pre-training, everything downstream would take care of itself. Now that most strong labs have bases that are roughly in the same tier, the question becomes: who can turn that raw capability into something that actually *does* things reliably in the real world?

For agents, I'd point to a few directions.

The first is the environment. In classic RLHF or even reasoning RL on math and code, the environment is fairly simple. You have a prompt, the model produces an answer, and you have a verifier or a reward model. With agents, the model is acting over long horizons, calling tools, reading feedback, recovering from errors. So building rich, diverse, realistic environments becomes a core research problem, maybe *the* core one. Whoever has better environments, with more variety and more faithful feedback, will get better generalization. It's a bit like data was for pre-training. Environments are the new data.

The second is reward and credit assignment over long trajectories. When a task takes fifty or a hundred steps, and you only find out at the end whether it succeeded, it's very hard to know which steps were good. Outcome-based rewards are clean but sparse. Process rewards are dense but noisy and easy to hack. I think there's a lot of room for methods that sit in between: partial verification, intermediate checkpoints, self-critique that's actually grounded.

The third is generalization rather than benchmark-fitting. It's very easy right now to over-train on a specific agent benchmark, a specific tool format, a specific scaffold, and get a nice number. But what we really want is a model that, when you drop it into an unfamiliar environment with unfamiliar tools, can still figure things out. That means we have to care about the diversity of tasks and avoid baking in too many assumptions about the harness.

And finally, I think efficiency matters more than people realize. Agent RL is expensive. Rollouts are long, environments are slow, and a lot of compute is spent waiting. So infrastructure, asynchronous rollouts, better sampling, deciding which trajectories are worth training on, these engineering questions end up being research questions too.

So my short answer is: the base model sets the ceiling, but post-training for agents decides how close you get to that ceiling, and right now that gap is still large. That's where I think the most interesting work is.

r001.rationale: The response discusses agent RL and post-training priorities, but identifies environments as the core research problem; it does not identify scaling reinforcement learning for agents as the central direction.

r002.rationale: The response describes the goal of reliable real-world agents and several open research areas, but does not clearly distinguish a known research objective from an unresolved path to achieve it.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the first thing to say is that "no generation gap" is a bit of a mixed blessing for people like me who work on post-training. For a long time, the honest answer to "why does your agent fall short" was "the base model is a generation behind." That excuse is gone now. The gap between what the strongest open base models can do and what the frontier labs' base models can do has narrowed to the point where, if your agent is bad, it's because of what you did after pretraining, not before. So the question becomes much more interesting and much more uncomfortable.

The way I think about it, post-training for agents has three layers, and the attention in the field is shifting from the first to the third.

The first layer is what I'd call "teaching the model to act." Tool calling formats, following a scaffold, producing well-formed actions. Two years ago this was most of the work. Today it's basically solved. Any decent base model learns it from a modest amount of SFT, and I don't think anyone should spend their research budget here anymore.

The second layer is reward design and environments. This is where most of the serious work is right now. If the model is strong enough to reason, then the bottleneck becomes: can you build environments where the signal is real? The hard part is not the RL algorithm. The hard part is that agentic tasks have long horizons, sparse outcomes, and a verifiability problem. For code, we have tests. For math, we have answers. For "go book my travel" or "do this research task," what is the reward? You end up building verifiers, and then the verifiers themselves become the research problem. I'd say the labs that are winning on agents right now are winning on environment construction and verifier quality, not on anything clever in the optimization.

The third layer is the one I find most intellectually interesting, which is what happens to the model's behavior over very long horizons. Once you train on multi-step tasks, you start to see things that don't show up in short-turn chat training. The model learns when to stop and ask, when to persist, when to back out of a bad plan. It learns a kind of epistemic honesty, or it fails to and learns to fake it. And this is where the fact that base models are strong actually makes things harder, not easier. A strong base model is very good at producing convincing-looking progress. If your reward can be gamed by convincing-looking progress, you will get an agent that is extremely persuasive and not very reliable. So I think a lot of the next few years is going to be about reliability rather than capability. Can the model tell you it failed? Can it tell you it's not sure? Does it hold up across a thousand steps and not just ten?

There's one more point I want to make, which is about data. When the base model gap closes, the thing that differentiates you is what the model has seen in post-training, and that increasingly means trajectories, not text. Real, messy, multi-turn trajectories of agents doing things, including failing. Whoever has the better flywheel for generating and filtering those trajectories is going to have the better agent. That's a systems and product problem as much as a research problem, and I think that's why you see the labs with deployed products pulling ahead on agents specifically. They have the loop.

So if I had to summarize: the research direction is moving from "how do we make the model capable" to "how do we make the model trustworthy over long horizons, and how do we build the environments and data flywheels that make that measurable." The base model being strong is the precondition for that work. It's not the finish line.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reward design, environments, and reliability, but does not identify scaling reinforcement learning for agents as the central research direction. It even says the hard part is not the RL algorithm.

r002.rationale: The response names goals and open challenges, but does not distinguish a clear research objective from an unresolved path to achieve it.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is what we mean by “no generation gap.” If we mean that the base models are at roughly comparable levels, then agent post-training becomes a place where differences can emerge. A model can be very good at answering a question and still struggle to complete a task that takes many steps.

For me, the research direction is to train on that whole process: deciding what to do, using a tool, checking the result, and adjusting when something goes wrong. You want the model to learn more than a successful sequence of actions. You want it to recognize when its approach has stopped working and recover.

That makes the training environment and the feedback particularly important. Can you tell whether the task was actually completed? Can you give useful feedback when success comes only after a long sequence of decisions? And can you prevent the model from learning shortcuts that work in the training environment but fail elsewhere?

I would put a lot of emphasis on generalization. If post-training improves performance only on familiar workflows, that is useful, but it is not yet a broadly capable agent. The more interesting result is an agent that can handle an unfamiliar task, discover what information it needs, and make reliable progress with limited time and resources. Comparable base models make those differences in learning and reliability more consequential.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes training the full task process, feedback, recovery, and generalization, but does not identify scaling reinforcement learning as the central research direction.

r002.rationale: It raises open questions about training and feedback, but does not distinguish a clear research objective from an unresolved path to achieve it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is what we mean by “no generation gap.” If the base models are at roughly the same level, then agent post-training becomes a way to differentiate them through how reliably they complete tasks.

For an agent, producing a good answer is only one part of the problem. It has to decide what to do next, use tools, interpret feedback, and recover when something goes wrong. A model can look very strong on individual steps and still fail over a long sequence of actions.

So I would focus on training in environments where we can evaluate the outcome of a complete task. The difficult parts are getting useful training signals, assigning credit across a long trajectory, and making sure the model learns strategies that transfer to unfamiliar tasks rather than memorizing an environment.

I wouldn’t assume that post-training can completely compensate for limitations in the base model. But if base capabilities are converging, the ability to turn those capabilities into consistent execution becomes a very important research direction.

r001.rationale: It discusses training agents for reliable task completion, but does not identify scaling reinforcement learning as the central research direction.

r002.rationale: It names challenges such as training signals and credit assignment, but does not clearly distinguish a known objective from an unresolved research path.
